extracted.intended_audience: general readers and writers of comic/satirical prose (Rabelaisian/Bacchic readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Producing lively, satirical, convivial prose in the Rabelais/Pantagruel vein aimed to amuse and exhilarate an audience of convivial readers; emphasizes action, robust diction, and targetting hypocrisy and pretension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to make readers merry
rubrics_metrics.description: "if you read them to make yourselves merry, as in manner of pastime I wrote them" — the author frames the work explicitly as written for pastime and merriment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write primarily to entertain; the work is a pastime meant to make readers merry. The author claims both writer and reader are 'far more worthy of pardon' when the aim is simple merriment, implying permissive license for playful or bawdy content when the intent is amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target hypocrisy and counterfeit sanctimony
rubrics_metrics.description: The author denounces "squint-minded fellows, dissembling and counterfeit saints, demure lookers, hypocrites, pretended zealots, tough friars, buskin-monks," presenting them as suitable objects of ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical attack should be aimed at pretence, hypocrisy, and false piety. Exposing such figures (their gluttony, vanity, or duplicity) is a legitimate comedic aim and a recurring thematic target in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match audience taste — prefer the 'proper, handsome, and perfect' over grotesque monstrosities
rubrics_metrics.description: "they took more pleasure and delight in things that were proper, handsome, and perfect, than in misshapen, monstrous, and ridiculous creatures" (example: Ptolemy's party-coloured slave and camel offended rather than pleased).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gratuitous grotesquerie that repels the intended audience; novelty for its own sake can backfire. Consider the sensibilities of your readers: novelty should be pleasurable or edifying rather than merely shocking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a convivial, Bacchic tone for the intended readership
rubrics_metrics.description: The prologue addresses "most illustrious drinkers" and repeatedly frames the writing as a 'barrel' of wine to be drunk by "honest tipplers, all honest gouty men"; writing is likened to wine that should 'relish' and 'exhilarate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a generous, convivial voice — rhetorical hospitality, warmth, and occasional bawdiness — when addressing a like-minded audience. Emphasize abundance, merriment, and shared pleasure; treat readers as guests rather than critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not force acceptance — allow voluntary reception
rubrics_metrics.description: "If you do not think it good, let it alone. I am not like those officious and importunate sots, who by force... constrain an easy good-natured fellow to whiffle, quaff, carouse... All honest tipplers... need not drink thereof if it please them not."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit readers to accept or reject the work freely; do not coerce or browbeat them into appreciation. The writer should offer his work in good faith and allow voluntary reception rather than aggressive persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribute actively rather than remain an idle spectator
rubrics_metrics.description: The author recounts Diogenes turning and furiously handling his tub so that he 'might not seem a loitering slug and lazy fellow' among busy citizens; he resolves not to be 'only an idle spectator' but to serve where he can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should engage actively with their subject and community: take a role (participant, commentator, servant of the public), produce useful or energizing material, and avoid passive detachment. Energetic engagement helps justify the comic voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exuberant, varied, and vigorous diction to animate comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Long catalogues of vigorous verbs describe Diogenes 'turn it, veer it, wheel it, whirl it... tramp it, stamp it, tap it, ting it...' demonstrating an energetic, piled-up style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ lively, varied language (repetition, long verb lists, onomatopoeic or physical verbs) to create comic momentum and vividness. Energetic diction and verbal piling can produce humor through rhythm, escalation, and sensory excess.
